metaTitle: Vamoose for Mice: What's in It, Does It Work?
metaDescription: Vamoose is a plant-oil scent pouch sold to repel mice, not kill them. See the label ingredients, what the evidence shows, and what to pair it with.
h1: Vamoose for Mice: What Is in the Pouches and What the Evidence Shows
dek: Vamoose is a scent repellent, and three different formulas carry the name. Here is what the labels list, what the maker claims, what research says about plant-oil repellents, and what to do alongside it.
excerpt: What Vamoose mouse repellent pouches contain according to their labels, what the maker claims, what research on plant-oil repellents shows, and what to pair them with.

quickAnswer.lead: **Vamoose is a scent repellent, not a mouse killer: pouches of carrier material scented with plant oils, sold without any EPA review of the claim that they work.** The two formulas with [labels on file in Washington State University's pesticide database](https://picol.cahnrs.wsu.edu/search?q=vamoose) contain 4.3% and 6% oil by weight. Research on plant-oil rodent repellents shows inconsistent results, so treat a pouch as an optional extra to sealing and trapping.
bullets: On both registered labels a pack holds 4 pouches of 1.5 oz (42.5 g) each, distributed by BugMD LLC.
The original label lists cornmint oil 4.0%, citronella oil 0.2% and linseed oil 0.1% on diatomaceous earth and calcium silicate.
The label filed as Vamoose PLUS lists peppermint oil 4%, clove oil 1%, lemongrass oil 0.5% and rosemary oil 0.5%.
Both labels say to replace pouches at least every 30 days and to keep them out of reach of children.
[EPA says it does not review products sold under the minimum-risk exemption](https://www.epa.gov/minimum-risk-pesticides/conditions-minimum-risk-pesticides), which is how Vamoose is sold.
A 2016 systematic review of 54 publications found inconsistent success for plant-based rodent repellents across lab, enclosure and field studies.

body.text: What is Vamoose for mice?

Vamoose is a pack of scented pouches distributed by BugMD LLC that is meant to repel mice and rats with the smell of plant oils; it does not trap, poison or kill them. Each pack holds 4 pouches of 1.5 oz (42.5 g), according to [the labels on file in Washington State University's PICOL pesticide database](https://picol.cahnrs.wsu.edu/search?q=vamoose). You set a pouch in an enclosed space and replace it when the scent fades.

The marketing makes two claims at once. The label says the smell drives rodents out of their hiding places, and [BugMD's own page for the pouches](https://bugmd.com/products/vamoose-newformula) says it stops rodents from entering in the first place. The same page states that the product does not kill rodents and describes it as prevention rather than elimination.

Vamoose belongs to the family of scent repellents, alongside peppermint sprays, granules and other pouch products. The [overview of mouse repellents by type](/blog/mice-repellent) compares that whole family, and the [complete mouse control reference](/learn/mice) shows where a repellent sits next to sealing, trapping and cleanup.

body.text: What ingredients are in Vamoose?

Vamoose pouches contain a small percentage of plant oils on a carrier material, and which oils depends on which of three formulas you have: cornmint, citronella and linseed in the original; peppermint, clove, lemongrass and rosemary in PLUS; and peppermint, cinnamon and cedarwood in Pro. Two of the three have labels registered with state regulators. The third, Vamoose Pro, is described only on the maker's website so far.

body.text: The maker's website does not keep these apart. The page for the standard pouches is titled as a new formula and headlines the four oils on the PLUS label, while its question-and-answer section still describes the original blend of cornmint, citronella and linseed oils on diatomaceous earth. [The Vamoose Pro page](https://bugmd.com/products/bugmd-vamoose-pro) describes the earlier product as leaning on a single oil. Neither product page gives a percentage for any individual oil.

The bag settles it. Under the federal rule this product is sold under, [EPA requires each active ingredient to be listed on the label by name and percentage by weight, and each inert ingredient by name](https://www.epa.gov/minimum-risk-pesticides/conditions-minimum-risk-pesticides). Read the panel on the package you are holding. The PLUS label on file adds a PLUS badge and a new-and-improved-formula burst to the front, but the maker's product page lists the four-oil formula simply as Vamoose rodent repelling pouches, so the ingredient list is the dependable way to tell the formulas apart.

The percentages translate into small amounts. By arithmetic from the label, a 1.5 oz (42.5 g) pouch at 4.3% oil holds about 1.8 g of oil, and at 6% about 2.55 g. That is roughly 0.06 to 0.09 oz per pouch. The rest is carrier. In the original formula the carrier is diatomaceous earth and calcium silicate; the label lists both as inert ingredients and makes no pest claim for either.
What does the maker claim, and what does the label warn about?

The maker claims the pouches repel mice and rats for up to 30 days and are safe around people and pets when used as directed; the label's own precautions say to keep them out of reach of children and that the contents may be harmful if swallowed. The claims below are the maker's, taken from the labels and the two product pages.

items: **Duration.** Up to 30 days per pouch. The label calls the pouches proven to protect for that long and does not say how that was established.
**How it is said to work.** A scent that overwhelms a rodent's sense of smell so that it leaves. The website calls this a scent barrier and a force field.
**No kill.** The website says nothing is killed and nothing needs cleaning up.
**Safety wording.** Safe around people and pets, with an asterisk that reads when used as directed.
**Vamoose Pro.** 33% more essential oil than the previous generation in a pouch that is 50% bigger, with pumice rock as a slow-release carrier.
**Refund.** A 30-day money-back offer is advertised on the maker's site.

body.text: One detail is worth noticing. The Pro page says that using three oils instead of leaning on one makes the smell hold up for weeks instead of fading in days. That sits awkwardly beside the 30-day claim printed on the earlier labels.
What the precautions say

Both labels carry the signal word Caution and the instruction to keep the product out of reach of children. The precautionary statements say the contents may be harmful if swallowed and may cause slight eye and skin irritation. The storage section says to keep it away from children and pets, in the original closed container, somewhere cool and dry, protected from freezing, out of direct sun and away from heat above 80°F.

The first-aid section says to rinse the mouth and drink plenty of water if the contents are swallowed, to rinse eyes with plenty of water, and to wash skin with soap and water. If irritation persists, it directs you to call a physician or Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222.

body.title: Safe when used as directed is a conditional claim
body.text: The label that says safe around people and pets also says keep out of reach of children and may be harmful if swallowed. Put pouches where a toddler, dog or cat cannot reach or chew them. If a pet chews one, call your veterinarian.
Is Vamoose registered or approved by the EPA?

No. Both labels state that the product has not been registered by the US Environmental Protection Agency and that BugMD represents it as qualifying for the exemption in section 25(b) of the federal pesticide law, known as FIFRA. The PICOL database lists both labels as Section 25(b) products.

[EPA's conditions for minimum risk pesticides](https://www.epa.gov/minimum-risk-pesticides/conditions-minimum-risk-pesticides) explain what that status means. A product is exempt from federal registration if it meets six conditions: its active ingredients come only from a list in the regulation, its inert ingredients come from permitted categories, every ingredient is on the label, it makes no claim to control organisms that threaten human health or insects or rodents carrying specific diseases, the label shows the producer's name and contact details, and the label carries no false or misleading statements. States may still require their own registration, and the database shows 2026 registrations for both labels in Washington and Oregon.

What matters to a buyer is what the exemption leaves out. EPA says on that page that it does not review exempted products. Under the exemption, no federal reviewer checks a claim such as 30 days of protection, the word proven, or the safety wording. That is not evidence that the pouches fail. It means the claims are the maker's own, with no federal review behind them.

The same page notes that the rule against false or misleading statements covers a producer's website and advertising as well as the label. EPA's examples include claims that imply a wider range of effectiveness than a product has, and wording that suggests a product contains no chemicals.
Is there independent evidence that these plant oils repel mice?

There is laboratory evidence that plant oils can affect rodent behavior, but the record across laboratory, enclosure and field studies is inconsistent, and no published trial of Vamoose itself turned up in the research for this page. A PubMed search for the product name in October 2026 returned nothing, and neither product page cites a study.

The best single summary is [a 2016 systematic review in the Journal of Chemical Ecology](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27613544/). Its authors screened 54 publications in which plant compounds or plants were tested on rodent behavior or metabolism. They reported that essential oils and terpenoids showed the strongest effects in laboratory experiments, consistently across species, and recommended systematic screening of those groups. They also reported inconsistent success across laboratory, enclosure and field studies, and tied that record to the small number of plant-based rodent repellents that had been registered.

Read closely, that supports a modest position. A strong plant smell is a reasonable thing to try, and in controlled tests such oils have changed what rodents do. A cage is not a kitchen. A mouse in a house has a nest, a food source it already knows and a choice of routes, and by the review's account an effect seen in one setting has not dependably shown up in the next.

body.text: Mint is the common thread. Peppermint oil is the largest ingredient on the PLUS label and the first oil named for Pro, and cornmint, the main oil in the original, is another mint, listed in the database as *Mentha arvensis*. The guide to [peppermint oil for mice](/blog/peppermint-oil-for-mice) goes through the research on that one oil, how quickly the smell fades and what it means for pets.
What can a scent repellent do, and what can it not do?

At best, a scent pouch may make one small, closed space less inviting for a few weeks; it cannot close an entry hole, remove food or a nest, or take a single mouse out of the house. The limits are easy to list, and most of them come straight from the maker and from federal rodent guidance.

items: **It may add a deterrent smell to an enclosed space.** That is the only kind of place the label directs it to, and how much difference it makes there has not been measured in any published trial found for this page.

**It cannot seal a gap.** [CDC says a mouse can fit through a hole the width of a pencil, 1/4 inch (6 mm) across](https://www.cdc.gov/healthy-pets/rodent-control/seal-up.html). A smell does nothing to that hole.
**It cannot remove what draws mice in.** The same CDC page says rodents are attracted to food and water and to convenient places to build nests. A pouch leaves all three where they are.
**It cannot lower the number of mice.** Nothing is caught or killed, as the maker says itself.
**It does not last.** The maker's site says essential oils fade naturally and tells buyers to replace pouches monthly.

body.text: The same limits apply to every product in this category, and some substitutes raise problems of their own. Mothballs come with legal and health questions that the guide to [whether mothballs keep mice away](/blog/do-mothballs-keep-mice-away) works through. Plug-in sound devices are a separate case, covered in the review of [whether ultrasonic pest repellers work](/blog/ultrasonic-pest-repellers-do-they-work).
How do you use Vamoose the way the label directs?
Use it as the label says: one or more pouches against the wall of a dry, enclosed space, replaced at least every 30 days, and kept where children and pets cannot get at them. In order:

items: Read the ingredient panel on your bag first, so you know which formula you have.
Pick enclosed spaces where mice hide or nest. The directions list sheds, attics, grills, pantries and garages, and the label's description adds basements, storage units, cars and RVs.
Set at least one pouch along the wall. The label says more pouches per area increase the effect, and it gives no number per room and no coverage in square feet.
Keep pouches dry. The label says the product is not intended for wet areas.
Put them where children and pets cannot reach or chew them, since the label warns that the contents may be harmful if swallowed.
Replace each pouch at least every 30 days, or earlier if you can no longer smell it.
Store spare pouches in the original closed container, somewhere cool and dry, out of direct sun and away from heat above 80°F.

body.text: The maker's website singles out vehicles, telling buyers to put pouches in attics, garages and especially inside car engines. The label names cars and RVs but gives no instructions about engine heat or moving parts, so ask the maker before leaving a pouch under the hood of a car you drive. The separate guide on [keeping mice out of a car](/blog/how-to-keep-mice-out-of-your-car) covers the steps that do not depend on a scent.
What should you pair with Vamoose to get rid of mice?
Pair it with sealing and trapping, because those are the steps that keep new mice out and remove the ones already inside. A pouch can sit alongside that work. It cannot stand in for it.
Seal the entry points

[CDC's seal-up guidance](https://www.cdc.gov/healthy-pets/rodent-control/seal-up.html) says to fill small holes with steel wool and put caulk around it to hold it in place, or to use spray foam, and to fix larger holes with lath screen or metal, cement, hardware cloth or metal sheeting. Its checklist includes the gaps around pipes under sinks, around doors and windows, behind appliances, around vents, and between the foundation and the ground. The guide to [steel wool for mouse holes](/blog/steel-wool-for-mice) explains which material suits which gap.
Take away the food

CDC's advice on food is specific. Keep food in thick plastic, metal or glass containers with tight lids, clean up spills right away, put pet food away after use and do not leave bowls out overnight, and keep indoor garbage in thick plastic or metal containers with tight lids. A pantry with a pouch on the shelf and an open bag of rice beside it is still a food source.
Remove the mice that are already inside

A repellent leaves the resident mice alive and in the building. Traps are what take them out, and the guide to [mouse traps by type](/blog/mice-traps) covers which to choose, how many to set and where to put them. Poison baits are a different kind of product altogether; read [what to know about mouse poison](/blog/mice-poison) before considering one. Readers who chose Vamoose because they do not want to kill anything will find the realistic options in [how to get rid of mice humanely](/blog/how-to-get-rid-of-mice-humanely).
Judge the result by signs, not by smell

If fresh droppings keep appearing, the mice are still there, however strong the pouch smells. The guide to [what mouse droppings look like](/blog/what-does-mouse-poop-look-like-canada) shows how to tell fresh from old. If sealing and trapping do not end the activity, or you cannot find how the mice get in, the page on [hiring a mouse exterminator](/blog/mice-exterminator) explains what a professional does and what to ask. For the wider range of hardware, the [rodent control product guides](/pest-product-guides/rodent-control) group the guides on traps, bait stations and exclusion in one place.
Is Vamoose worth using for mice?

As the only response to mice already living in a house, no: nothing on the label, on the maker's pages or in the published research shows that a scent pouch ends an infestation. As an optional extra in a dry, closed space, after the gaps are sealed and the traps have gone quiet, it is a judgment call, made knowing that the benefit is unproven.

body.text: One practical point is easy to miss. The label calls for replacement at least every 30 days, so a pouch is a recurring purchase for as long as you want the scent, and the maker's site steers buyers toward a subscription. A sealed gap does not need a refill.

faqs.question: Does Vamoose kill mice?
faqs.answer: No. Vamoose is a scent repellent, and the maker's own product page says it does not kill rodents. The pouches hold a carrier material scented with plant oils, and the label lists no rodent poison. That also means a pouch does not reduce the number of mice in a house. If mice are already living indoors, the ones present stay alive until they are trapped or leave on their own, which is why a repellent is normally paired with traps and with sealing the gaps they use.

faqs.question: How long does a Vamoose pouch last?
faqs.answer: The label says to replace each pouch at least every 30 days, or sooner when the scent can no longer be detected, and the maker claims up to 30 days of protection per pouch. No independent data on how long the scent or any effect lasts was found for this page. The maker's website says essential oils fade naturally. In practice the label's own test is your nose: once you cannot smell the pouch, the label treats it as due for replacement.

faqs.question: Is Vamoose safe around dogs, cats and children?
faqs.answer: The label says safe around people and pets when used as directed. It also carries the signal word Caution, says to keep the product out of reach of children, warns that the contents may be harmful if swallowed and may cause slight eye and skin irritation, and says to store it away from children and pets. Place pouches where a child or animal cannot reach or chew them. If a person swallows the contents, follow the label's first aid and call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222. If a pet chews a pouch, call your veterinarian.

faqs.question: What is the difference between Vamoose, Vamoose PLUS and Vamoose Pro?
faqs.answer: They are three formulas. The original label lists cornmint oil 4.0%, citronella oil 0.2% and linseed oil 0.1% on diatomaceous earth and calcium silicate. The label filed as Vamoose PLUS lists peppermint oil 4%, clove oil 1%, lemongrass oil 0.5% and rosemary oil 0.5% with calcium carbonate, vanillin and beeswax. The maker describes Vamoose Pro as peppermint, cinnamon and cedarwood oils on pumice rock in an 8% blend. The PLUS label on file adds a PLUS badge to the front of the pack, but the product name is otherwise the same, so check the ingredient panel.

faqs.question: Will Vamoose get mice out of walls or an attic?
faqs.answer: There is no published evidence that it will. The label says the scent drives rodents out of hiding places, but that claim has not been reviewed by EPA, and research on plant-based rodent repellents shows inconsistent results across laboratory, enclosure and field studies. Mice in a wall or attic have a nest and a route to food. Removing them takes traps, and keeping them out takes sealing the gaps they use, which can be as small as 1/4 inch across. A pouch can be added to an attic afterward as an optional extra.

faqs.question: Can I put Vamoose in my car's engine bay?
faqs.answer: The label lists cars and RVs among the places to put a pouch, and the maker's website suggests the engine compartment in particular. Neither gives data for vehicles, and the label has no instructions about engine heat or moving parts. It does say the product is not intended for wet areas and that spare pouches should be stored away from heat above 80 degrees Fahrenheit. Ask the maker before leaving a pouch under the hood of a car you drive, and do not rely on scent alone to protect wiring.
